# Branch Summaries

A `trxns` branch can contain many field vectors from earlier payments and the
latest payment. Reduction determines how much of that encoded collection
reaches the parent. It follows the
[field interactions](field-interactions.qmd) within the branch.

This explanation follows the
[pinned 0.2.4 reduction implementation](https://github.com/relflow/relflow/blob/8d9d6cfd8ce22a7819c2b5392c710d4f2cbe1a7c/src/relflow/architecture/pool.py).

## Choose What Reaches The Parent

| Reduction | Context passed to the parent | Main tradeoff |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `rf.Attention(n_outputs=K)` | `K` learned summary vectors | Learns which evidence to collect into a limited context. |
| `rf.Mean()` | One average of present token vectors | Simple and parameter-free at the reduction step. |
| `None` | The encoded token sequence | Retains more detail and increases the parent's token count. |

These choices concern reduction. A mean reduction can still follow a learned
branch encoder. Configure the branch's attention separately; see the
[Branch reference](../../data-types/branch.qmd#reduce-branch-memory).

Learned attention starts with trainable query vectors. Each query attends to the
branch's present memory and collects a summary. Multiple outputs provide
multiple learned views of the same history; their meanings emerge during
training.

## Why An Average Loses Multiplicity

An attention head combines values with normalized weights:

$$
s = \sum_i \alpha_i v_i, \qquad \sum_i \alpha_i = 1.
$$

If every value vector is the same vector $v$, this expression returns $v$
whether the memory contains one copy or many. A mean has the same limitation.
This is a statement about that normalized combination of identical values.
Other parts of a network, including positional signals and earlier encoder
updates, can supply information about sequence length.

At a common account-review cutoff, multiplicity may matter: several retained
payments can carry different evidence from one payment even when their
merchants and amounts are identical. RelFlow's learned branch reduction
includes additive evidence alongside attention.

## Additive Evidence

The learned reduction adds two trainable contributions to each normalized
attention summary:

- A projection of the sum of present branch input vectors, scaled by the square
  root of the configured capacity.
- A learned direction scaled by the number of present tokens divided by that
  capacity.

Both contributions start at zero, so training decides how much to use them.
The branch provides the additive evidence from its tokens before the sequence
encoder; these tokens already include any coordinate attention. Absent tokens
contribute neither values nor counts.

The count here is a **token count**. Fields can supply several tokens, and
nested branch outputs can add further tokens. It is not directly a count of
transactions or a sum of payment amounts. The model must learn how those
vector and count signals relate to each transaction's dispute target for the
30 days after the common review cutoff.

This mechanism supplies information that a normalized average can discard. It
does not make the model an exact calculator or guarantee extrapolation to
longer histories. Use the [canonical proofs](../../proofs.qmd) to inspect
recorded evidence, and validate the reduction choice on the application's
held-out observations.
